sections.heading: Continuous systems and modeling strategy
paragraphs: A continuous-state model describes variables evolving over continuous time; its input and output need not be identical or constant. Page 5 incorrectly claims signals are the same and do not vary. Applications listed include dam and tunnel engineering, missile trajectories, airport passenger flow, and business planning.

Translate the system into quantitative equations, then choose a numerical implementation. State variables must collectively capture the relevant dynamics to the accuracy required; state equations describe their change, often with time as the independent variable. Output equations specify quantities requested by users.

sections.heading: Reservoir and differential-equation classes
paragraphs: For the slide’s ideal infinite-capacity reservoir, q is the contents, x is signed input rate, dq/dt = x(t), and y = q. Thus q(t) = q(0) + integral from 0 to t of x(s) ds; if q(0)=4 and x=2 for three time units, q(3)=10.

The slides classify predator–prey models as first-order ODEs, orbital motion and RLC circuits as second-order ODEs, and wave or heat models as PDEs. A second-order ODE can be expressed as a first-order system by introducing velocity as another state.

sections.heading: Orbit states and outputs
paragraphs: For a planetary orbit the state vector contains three-dimensional position and velocity. Position derivatives are velocities; under the slide’s central-gravity model acceleration is −GM r-vector/|r-vector|³. The state can be used to calculate desired outputs such as distance or speed.

sections.heading: Predator–prey dynamics
paragraphs: With prey x and predators y, the general model is dx/dt = x f(x,y), dy/dt = y g(x,y). For positive populations, f and g are per-capita growth rates. Increasing predators suppresses prey growth; increasing prey supports predator growth. The qualitative cycle goes from abundant prey to more predators, falling prey, predator starvation, and prey recovery.

The Lotka–Volterra choice is f=b−py and g=rx−d, giving dx/dt=x(b−py) and dy/dt=y(rx−d). With positive parameters the positive equilibrium is (x,y)=(d/r,b/p). For b=p=r=d=1 it is (1,1), matching the slide’s phase-plane example.

For positive x,y the conserved quantity is C=b ln(y)−py−rx+d ln(x). Page 16 omits r before x; its expression is valid when r=1, as on page 17. The correction follows by differentiating C using the two state equations. Parameter values and initial conditions determine the trajectory.

sections.heading: Numerical integration
paragraphs: Forward Euler approximates the derivative using the current slope: x(n+1)=x(n)+h f(t(n),x(n)). For x′=x, x(0)=1 and h=0.2, one Euler step gives 1.2.

The slide’s Runge–Kutta formula is the explicit midpoint RK2 method: t_mid=t0+h/2, x_mid=x0+(h/2)f(t0,x0), then x1=x0+h f(t_mid,x_mid). For the same example, x_mid=1.1 and x1=1.22. These are approximations, not exact solutions.

sections.heading: MATLAB scripts, functions, input and output
paragraphs: Scripts and function files both use the .m extension. Scripts execute commands in the workspace; functions can take inputs, return outputs, and use local internal variables. The editor can be opened with edit or edit followed by a filename.

input("Enter a number") reads a numerical expression; input("Enter text", "s") reads text. disp(X) displays a value without the variable name, whereas fprintf supports formatted output such as %s for text and %d for an integer; \n produces a newline.

sections.heading: MATLAB arrays and plots
paragraphs: Examples include row vectors a=1:2, column vectors b=(1:3)' and matrix addition A+B. The example with a and b uses compatible implicit expansion to form a 3-by-2 result.

To graph a function, define x and y, then use plot(x,y). xlabel, ylabel, title, and grid on annotate the figure; axis equal uses equal scales and axis square makes the plot box square. A LineSpec can specify color, line style, and marker.

sections.heading: MATLAB selection and loops
paragraphs: if, elseif, else and end select branches; switch selects cases and otherwise handles unmatched cases. The age example on page 62 misclassifies age 20 and can classify nonpositive ages as senior; age 60 is correctly classified as senior. Check boundaries explicitly rather than copying it.

The page 61 parity example is erroneous: % starts a MATLAB comment, not a remainder operation, and both branches print Even number. Use mod(x,2)==0 for even integers and print Odd number in the other branch.
menu displays choices and returns the selected button number. A for loop iterates over a supplied sequence such as 1:10 or 1.0:-0.2:0.0; a while loop repeats while its condition is true.
A MATLAB function can be declared as function area = calcarea(rad), assign its output with area = pi * rad * rad, and end with end. A caller can use calcarea(5) or assign area = calcarea(radius).
